title.title: Divergent reciprocal sums force long progressions
title.subtitle: Claim: if $\sum_{a \in A} 1/a = \infty$, then $A$ has arithmetic progressions of every finite length

plain: Take whole numbers, not too sparse (like the primes): you always find evenly spaced runs, as long as you like

beats.text: $\textsf{Erd\H{o}s}$ asked: does $\sum 1/a = \infty$, as for the primes, force progressions of every length?
That needs $r_k(N)/N$ below $(\log N)^{-1-\epsilon}$; for $k \ge 5$ the best bound was not
Schematic curves. The claim: $C_k\,e^{-c_k(\log N)^{\varepsilon_k}}$ for every $k \ge 3$

steps: Suppose a dense set has no long progression
Then it is denser on some structured piece: zoom in there
Repeat; density cannot grow forever, so a progression appears
Adding up over scales gives the reciprocal-sum statement

achievement.label: Reciprocal-sum conjecture (1974), erdosproblems #3
statement: \textstyle\sum_{a \in A} \frac1a = \infty \;\Rightarrow\; A \text{ has } k\text{-term APs for every } k
achievement.context: Before: only $k = 3$ had a strong enough bound (Kelley–Meka, 2023)
achievement.note: Lean reaches the corollary by a weaker bound; Theorem 1.1 is unchecked

verify.detail: In Lean: the $\textsf{Erd\H{o}s}$ statement, via $N e^{-c(\log\log N)^{1+\eta}}$. Not Theorem 1.1
verify.ourCheck: We read the Lean statement; we did not build it

voice.text: If reciprocals sum to infinity, must a set hold evenly spaced runs of every length?
No run means a denser piece. Zoom in and repeat until one must appear.

sources.quote: What the conjecture needs is a Szemerédi bound $r_k(N)$ that decays faster than $N/(\log N)^{1+\epsilon}$
For $k \ge 5$ the best was Leng, Sah and Sawhney's $N \exp(-(\log \log N)^{c})$ from 2024, which is not summable over dyadic scales
The quantitative Theorem 1.1 is NOT a comparator target
